guides.title: Choking (adult)
guides.overview: Choking occurs when a foreign object blocks the airway, making it difficult or impossible to breathe. Act fast — a blocked airway can cause unconsciousness within minutes.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance immediately if the person loses consciousness or the object cannot be dislodged after several attempts.

stepsDetail.title: Ask if they can cough
stepsDetail.description: If the person can speak, cough forcefully, or breathe, encourage them to keep coughing. A strong cough is the most effective way to clear the blockage — do not interfere.

stepsDetail.title: Lean them forward & give 5 back blows
stepsDetail.description: Stand to the side and slightly behind. Support their chest with one hand, lean them forward, then strike firmly 5 times between the shoulder blades using the heel of your other hand.

stepsDetail.title: Give 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich)
stepsDetail.description: Stand behind the person. Make a fist with one hand just above their navel and below the chest. Grip with your other hand and pull sharply inward and upward. Repeat 5 times.

stepsDetail.title: Alternate until cleared
stepsDetail.description: Continue alternating 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object is dislodged or the person can breathe, speak, or cough effectively on their own.

stepsDetail.title: If they collapse — call Ambulance & start CPR
stepsDetail.description: If the person becomes unconscious, lower them carefully to the ground. Call Ambulance immediately and begin CPR. Before each rescue breath, look in the mouth and remove any visible object only if clearly seen.

guides.title: Choking (infant)
guides.overview: Infants can choke silently because their airway is small. Use gentle, firm back blows and chest thrusts only; do not use abdominal thrusts on a baby under 12 months.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance immediately if the baby cannot cry, cough, breathe, or becomes limp or unconscious.

stepsDetail.title: Check breathing and call for help
stepsDetail.description: If the baby cannot cry, cough, or breathe, shout for help. Ask someone nearby to call Ambulance while you begin first aid.

stepsDetail.title: Give 5 back blows
stepsDetail.description: Lay the baby face down along your forearm with the head lower than the chest. Support the head and jaw, then give 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

stepsDetail.title: Give 5 chest thrusts
stepsDetail.description: Turn the baby face up, still keeping the head lower than the chest. Place two fingers in the centre of the chest and press sharply downward 5 times.

stepsDetail.title: Repeat and start CPR if needed
stepsDetail.description: Alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts until the object clears. If the baby becomes unconscious, begin infant CPR and keep checking the mouth for a visible object.

guides.title: Burns treatment
guides.overview: Burns can keep damaging skin after the heat source is gone. Cooling the area quickly reduces pain, swelling, and the depth of injury.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance for burns to the face, hands, genitals, large areas, chemical or electrical burns, or if the person has trouble breathing.

stepsDetail.title: Move away from danger
stepsDetail.description: Stop the burning process. Move the person away from flames, hot liquids, steam, chemicals, or electricity only when it is safe for you to do so.

stepsDetail.title: Cool with running water
stepsDetail.description: Hold the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste, or powders.

stepsDetail.title: Remove tight items
stepsDetail.description: Remove rings, watches, belts, or tight clothing near the burn before swelling starts. Do not remove anything stuck to the skin.

stepsDetail.title: Cover the burn loosely
stepsDetail.description: Cover the cooled burn with clean plastic wrap or a sterile non-stick dressing. Keep it loose and avoid bursting blisters.

stepsDetail.title: Treat for shock
stepsDetail.description: Keep the person warm, calm, and seated or lying down. Raise their legs if they feel faint, unless this causes pain or breathing difficulty.

guides.title: CPR / no pulse
guides.overview: CPR (Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation) keeps blood and oxygen moving when the heart stops. Every second without CPR reduces survival chances — begin immediately and do not wait for emergency services.
guides.warning: Do not stop CPR until paramedics arrive, an AED is ready to use, or the person starts breathing normally. If you are untrained in rescue breaths, perform hands-only CPR with continuous chest compressions.

stepsDetail.title: Check safety & response
stepsDetail.description: Make sure the area is safe. Tap the person's shoulders firmly and shout 'Are you OK?' If there is no response, shout for help and call Ambulance — or ask a bystander to call while you begin.

stepsDetail.title: Lay flat & open the airway
stepsDetail.description: Place the person on their back on a firm, flat surface. Tilt the head back gently and lift the chin to open the airway. Look, listen, and feel for breathing for no more than 10 seconds.

stepsDetail.title: Give 30 chest compressions
stepsDetail.description: Place the heel of one hand on the centre of the chest, then your other hand on top. Press down at least 5–6 cm at a rate of 100–120 per minute. Allow the chest to fully rise between each compression.

stepsDetail.title: Give 2 rescue breaths
stepsDetail.description: Tilt the head back, pinch the nose shut, and seal your mouth over theirs. Breathe steadily for 1 second and watch for chest rise. Give a second breath, then return to compressions immediately.

stepsDetail.title: Continue the 30:2 cycle
stepsDetail.description: Maintain 30 compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths without stopping. If an AED arrives, apply it as soon as possible and follow every voice instruction it gives.

stepsDetail.title: Keep going until help takes over
stepsDetail.description: Do not stop unless emergency services take over, the person starts breathing normally on their own, an AED advises you to stop, or you are physically unable to continue.

guides.title: Fainting / collapse
guides.overview: Fainting is usually a short loss of consciousness caused by reduced blood flow to the brain. Most people recover quickly, but collapse can also signal a serious emergency.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance if the person is not fully awake within 1 minute, has chest pain, trouble breathing, injury from the fall, seizure, pregnancy, diabetes, or repeated fainting.

stepsDetail.title: Lay them flat
stepsDetail.description: Help the person lie on their back. If they fell, check for injury before moving them.

stepsDetail.title: Raise the legs
stepsDetail.description: Lift their legs about 30 cm if it does not cause pain. Loosen tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist.

stepsDetail.title: Check breathing and recovery
stepsDetail.description: Make sure they are breathing normally. When they wake, keep them lying down for several minutes and help them sit up slowly.

stepsDetail.title: Do not give food immediately
stepsDetail.description: Do not give food or drink until they are fully alert. If they vomit, turn them on their side to keep the airway clear.

guides.title: Fracture & dislocation
guides.overview: A fracture or dislocation can worsen if the injured part is moved. The goal is to keep it still, reduce swelling, and get medical care.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance for open fractures, severe pain, loss of feeling, blue or cold fingers or toes, spine injury, heavy bleeding, or if the limb looks badly deformed.

stepsDetail.title: Keep the person still
stepsDetail.description: Ask the person not to move the injured area. Support it in the position you found it and avoid trying to straighten bones or joints.

stepsDetail.title: Control bleeding
stepsDetail.description: If there is bleeding, apply gentle pressure around the wound with a clean cloth. Do not press directly on exposed bone.

stepsDetail.title: Immobilize the injury
stepsDetail.description: Use a padded splint, folded cloth, or sling to prevent movement above and below the injury. Tie supports snugly but not tightly.

stepsDetail.title: Apply cold gently
stepsDetail.description: Wrap ice or a cold pack in cloth and place it near the injury for up to 20 minutes to reduce swelling. Do not put ice directly on skin.

stepsDetail.title: Watch circulation
stepsDetail.description: Check fingers or toes for warmth, colour, and sensation. Loosen bandages if they become numb, cold, blue, or increasingly painful.

guides.title: Severe bleeding
guides.overview: Severe bleeding can become life-threatening within minutes. Direct pressure is the most important first step.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance immediately if bleeding is spurting, does not slow with firm pressure, soaks through dressings, or follows a major injury.

stepsDetail.title: Apply firm direct pressure
stepsDetail.description: Press hard on the wound with a clean cloth, gauze, or your gloved hand. Keep steady pressure without repeatedly lifting the dressing to check.

stepsDetail.title: Lay them down
stepsDetail.description: Help the person lie down. If possible, raise the bleeding area above heart level while maintaining pressure.

stepsDetail.title: Add more dressings
stepsDetail.description: If blood soaks through, place another dressing on top and keep pressing. Do not remove the first dressing because it may disturb clotting.

stepsDetail.title: Use a tourniquet only for extreme limb bleeding
stepsDetail.description: If bleeding from an arm or leg cannot be controlled and help is delayed, apply a tourniquet above the wound if trained. Note the time and do not loosen it.

guides.title: Choking with CPR
guides.overview: If a choking person becomes unconscious, CPR helps move air and may dislodge the object. Do not blindly sweep inside the mouth.
guides.warning: Call Ambulance immediately before starting CPR if you are alone with an adult. For a child or infant, give about 2 minutes of CPR first if no one else can call.

stepsDetail.title: Lower them safely
stepsDetail.description: Support the person to the ground and lay them on their back on a firm, flat surface. Shout for help and call Ambulance.

stepsDetail.title: Open the airway
stepsDetail.description: Tilt the head back and lift the chin. Look inside the mouth. Remove an object only if you can clearly see it and reach it easily.

stepsDetail.title: Start chest compressions
stepsDetail.description: Place your hands in the centre of the chest and give 30 firm compressions at 100 to 120 per minute. Let the chest fully rise between compressions.

stepsDetail.title: Check the mouth again
stepsDetail.description: After compressions, open the airway and look for a visible object. Remove it only if clearly seen. Do not push fingers blindly into the throat.

stepsDetail.title: Try 2 rescue breaths
stepsDetail.description: Pinch the nose, seal your mouth over theirs, and give 2 breaths. If the chest does not rise, reposition the head and continue compressions.

stepsDetail.title: Repeat 30:2 cycles
stepsDetail.description: Continue cycles of 30 compressions and 2 breaths, checking for a visible object before breaths each time.

stepsDetail.title: Continue until help arrives
stepsDetail.description: Keep going until emergency services take over, the person starts breathing normally, or you are physically unable to continue.
